blocks.text: A weld on a pressure-vessel nozzle must be checked without cutting it open, and without taking it out of service. Four techniques are available, each sensitive to a different kind of flaw. Choosing the wrong one means looking straight at a defect and not seeing it.

blocks.markdown: Non-destructive testing (NDT) detects flaws without damaging the part. No method finds everything. Each exploits a physical effect that a flaw disturbs: liquid drawn into an opening, magnetic flux that leaks around a break, sound that reflects from an interface, or radiation absorbed differently by a void. The right choice depends on the type of flaw, where it lies (on the surface or within the volume), the material and the geometry.

rows: Dye penetrant (PT)
Liquid enters surface openings by capillary action; developer draws it out as a visible indication
Surface-breaking cracks, laps, porosity in any non-porous material
Surface must be clean and open; no subsurface flaws
Magnetic particle (MT)
Flux leaks at a flaw in a magnetised part and attracts iron particles
Surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic materials
Only ferromagnetic materials; field must cross the flaw
Ultrasonic (UT)
Sound pulse reflects from interfaces; time of flight gives depth
Internal planar flaws and cracks; flaw depth and size
Needs a couplant, skilled interpretation; rough or complex surfaces are hard
Radiographic (RT)
X- or gamma rays are attenuated less through a void than through metal
Volumetric flaws: porosity, inclusions, voids; cracks aligned with the beam
Radiation safety; planar flaws perpendicular to the beam are missed
blocks.caption: Four common methods and what they find.

blocks.markdown: **Why surface-breaking cracks suit penetrant and magnetic particle testing.** A fatigue crack nucleates at the surface, where the stress is usually highest, and is open to it. Penetrant testing relies on capillary action to draw a low-viscosity, high-wetting liquid into a very narrow opening; after the excess is wiped off, a developer pulls the liquid back out, so the crack appears as a bright or coloured line far wider than the crack itself. This works only if the crack is open to the surface. In magnetic particle testing, a crack interrupts the magnetic flux in the part, forcing flux to leak out of the surface across the gap. Fine iron particles collect there. The effect is strongest when the crack is perpendicular to the field and close to the surface, so the part is magnetised in two directions.

blocks.title: Surface methods: summary
blocks.text: PT and MT are cheap, quick and very sensitive to tight surface-breaking cracks. PT works on any non-porous material; MT works only on ferromagnetic steels but also finds near-surface flaws and cracks filled with contaminant. Neither shows depth, and neither finds internal flaws.

blocks.markdown: **Ultrasonic pulse-echo.** A probe sends a short pulse of sound into the part. The pulse travels at the material's wave speed $v$ until it meets an interface, such as a crack face or the back wall, and part of it reflects back to the probe. The instrument measures the time $t$ between the pulse and the echo. Since the sound travels to the flaw and back, the one-way distance is half of the total path.

blocks.caption: Flaw depth $d$ from a pulse-echo time $t$ and wave speed $v$ (longitudinal waves in steel $\approx5900$ m/s; in aluminium $\approx6300$ m/s; typical values). The factor 2 accounts for the round trip.

blocks.title: Flaw depth from the echo time
blocks.prompt: A longitudinal probe on a steel forging ($v=5900$ m/s, typical) records a flaw echo $12.4\ \mu\text{s}$ after the transmit pulse. How deep is the flaw?
blocks.answer: The flaw is about 36.6 mm deep.

blocks.title: Flaw echo and back-wall echo
blocks.prompt: On a steel plate ($v=5900$ m/s), the display shows a flaw echo at $6.8\ \mu\text{s}$ and the back-wall echo at $17.0\ \mu\text{s}$. Find the flaw depth and the plate thickness, and decide whether the flaw is near the surface or the back wall.

steps.text: The flaw lies at 40 percent of the thickness, so it is in the upper two-fifths of the plate, on the probe side.

blocks.answer: Flaw depth about 20.1 mm in a plate of about 50.1 mm thickness.

items: Match the method to the flaw's location and orientation first, then to the material.
Penetrant needs a clean, open crack; magnetic particle needs a ferromagnetic part and a field that crosses the crack.
For ultrasonics, check the wave speed for the material and always halve the round-trip path.

blocks.title: Absence of an indication is not proof of absence of a flaw
blocks.text: Every method has a minimum detectable size and an orientation to which it is blind. A clean result with the wrong method, or with an uncalibrated instrument, gives false confidence.

points: PT, MT, UT and RT detect surface-breaking, near-surface, internal planar and volumetric flaws respectively; MT needs ferromagnetic material.
Surface-breaking cracks suit PT (capillary action) and MT (flux leakage across the opening).

questions.stem: A fatigue crack is suspected on the surface of an aluminium bracket. Which method is the most appropriate?

options.text: Magnetic particle testing
Radiography of the whole bracket
Dye penetrant testing
Hardness testing

distractorRationale.b: Radiography is poor at finding tight planar cracks.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: penetrant works on non-magnetic surface cracks.

questions.explanation: Surface-breaking cracks are found well by penetrant testing, which works on any non-porous material. Magnetic particle testing is limited to ferromagnetic steels, so it cannot be used on aluminium.

questions.stem: Which method is best suited to detecting gas porosity inside a casting?

options.text: Dye penetrant
Magnetic particle
Visual inspection of the surface
Radiography

distractorRationale.b: MT finds surface and near-surface flaws.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: voids are volumetric and absorb less radiation.

questions.explanation: Internal voids absorb less radiation than the surrounding metal, so they appear on the film or detector. The surface methods cannot see inside the casting.

questions.stem: In magnetic particle testing, why is the part magnetised in two directions?

options.text: Because one direction demagnetises the part
Because the particles need two fields to form
Because a crack is detected best when it is perpendicular to the field, and cracks may lie in any direction
Because the field is not needed

questions.correctOptionText: Because a crack is detected best when it is perpendicular to the field, and cracks may lie in any direction

distractorRationale.b: Particles form in a single field.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: flux leakage is strongest across a crack.

questions.explanation: A crack parallel to the magnetic field disturbs it very little and gives no leakage. Two field directions make sure that cracks of any orientation cross at least one of them.

questions.stem: Why does penetrant testing only find flaws that break the surface?

options.text: The developer cannot cross a thin surface layer
The liquid must be drawn into the opening by capillary action
The liquid is magnetic
Sound is needed to bring up the indication

questions.correctOptionText: The liquid must be drawn into the opening by capillary action

distractorRationale.a: The developer is not the limit.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: capillary entry needs an opening at the surface.

questions.explanation: The method relies on capillary action to draw penetrant into the flaw. A subsurface flaw has no opening, so the liquid never enters and no indication forms.

questions.stem: An inspector computes the flaw depth as $vt$ instead of $vt/2$. What error results?

options.text: The depth is underestimated by a factor of 2
The depth is overestimated by a factor of 2
The depth is unchanged
The depth is off by the square root of 2

questions.correctOptionText: The depth is overestimated by a factor of 2

distractorRationale.b: Correct: the sound travels to the flaw and back.
distractorRationale.d: The round trip is exactly twice the depth.

questions.explanation: The measured time covers the path to the flaw and back, so the path length is twice the depth. Without the factor of one half the computed depth is double the true value.

questions.stem: A pulse-echo probe on steel ($v=5900$ m/s) shows a flaw echo at $8.0\ \mu\text{s}$. Find the flaw depth in mm.
questions.explanation: $d=vt/2=5900\times8.0\times10^{-6}/2=0.0236$ m, or 23.6 mm. The time must be in seconds.

questions.stem: A probe on an aluminium casting ($v=6300$ m/s, typical) records a flaw echo at $3.5\ \mu\text{s}$. Find the flaw depth in mm.
questions.explanation: $d=6300\times3.5\times10^{-6}/2=0.01103$ m, which is 11.03 mm. This is a shallow flaw, in the near-surface part of the casting.

questions.stem: A steel plate is known to be 40 mm thick. The back-wall echo arrives at $13.6\ \mu\text{s}$ and a flaw echo arrives at $7.1\ \mu\text{s}$. Calibrate the wave speed from the back wall and then find the flaw depth in mm.
questions.explanation: From the back wall, $v=2\times0.040/13.6\times10^{-6}=5882$ m/s. Then $d=vt/2=5882\times7.1\times10^{-6}/2=0.02088$ m, which is 20.88 mm. Equivalently, the flaw lies at $7.1/13.6$ of the thickness.

questions.stem: Explain why surface-breaking cracks are well suited to detection by dye penetrant and magnetic particle methods, and state one limitation of each.
markingGuide: Penetrant: capillary action draws liquid into the open crack, developer draws it out to give a wide visible line
Magnetic particle: crack interrupts flux; leakage at the surface attracts iron particles; best when the crack is perpendicular to the field and near the surface
Penetrant limitation: cannot detect subsurface or closed/smeared cracks, surface must be clean
Magnetic particle limitation: only ferromagnetic materials, and cracks parallel to the field are missed
questions.explanation: Both methods depend on the crack being open at the surface: penetrant needs an opening to fill, and a magnetic leakage field needs the break to be near the surface. Neither can see deep internal flaws.

questions.stem: Select a suitable NDT method for each of the following and justify the choice: (i) tight fatigue crack at the surface of a ferritic steel shaft; (ii) lack-of-fusion planar flaw 25 mm deep in a thick steel weld; (iii) gas pores in an aluminium casting; (iv) a surface crack on a titanium blade.
markingGuide: (i) Magnetic particle (or penetrant): ferromagnetic, surface-breaking, high sensitivity
(ii) Ultrasonic: planar internal flaw, reflects sound, depth from time
(iv) Dye penetrant: titanium is non-ferromagnetic, so MT is not applicable
Mentions limitations such as the need for a clean surface for PT or orientation dependence
questions.explanation: Match the flaw location and the material: surface and ferromagnetic gives MT, surface and non-magnetic gives PT, internal planar gives UT, and internal volumetric gives RT. The same logic helps when a part could be checked by more than one method.
